name: Electric charge
kicker: Positive or negative property of matter · Measured in coulombs
dates: Two kinds named positive and negative by Franklin, 1740s
briefing: Electric charge is a basic property of matter that comes in two kinds, positive and negative, names chosen by Benjamin Franklin. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, which is why a balloon rubbed on your hair can stick to a wall. Charge is measured in coulombs, and every proton and electron carries the same tiny amount, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs: positive for the proton, negative for the electron.
answerHtml: electric charge (accept charge; prompt on q; do not accept “electric current” or “elementary charge”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1733, Charles du Fay [“dew FAY”] described two kinds of this property, calling one “vitreous” because it came from rubbed glass and the other “resinous” because it came from rubbed amber and other resins. Benjamin Franklin later gave those two kinds new names.
tossups.r: Like kinds repel and opposite kinds attract. For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, that comes in positive and negative forms.

tossups.p: Quarks carry fractions of this property, such as plus two-thirds or minus one-third of a proton’s amount, but they are never found alone. In a neutral atom, the positive amount of this property on the protons exactly balances the negative amount on the electrons.
tossups.r: Opposite kinds of it attract. For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs.

tossups.p: The Faraday constant, about 96,485 coulombs per mole, is the total amount of this property carried by a mole of electrons. Gauss’s law says the electric flux through any closed surface equals the amount of this property inside, divided by the permittivity of free space.
tossups.r: It is measured in coulombs. For 10 points, name this property of matter that comes in positive and negative kinds.

tossups.p: In 1785, Charles-Augustin de Coulomb [“KOO-lohm”] used a torsion balance to show that the force between two small objects carrying this property falls off with the square of the distance between them. That force is proportional to the product of the two amounts of this property.
tossups.r: Its SI unit is named for Coulomb. For 10 points, name this property, which can be positive or negative.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin pictured electricity as a single fluid, calling an object with too much of that fluid positive and an object with too little negative. In an isolated system, the total amount of this property never changes, because it is conserved.
tossups.r: Objects with the same kind of it repel each other. For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs.

tossups.p: Thales [“THAY-leez”] of Miletus is said to have noticed that amber rubbed with fur attracts bits of straw, and William Gilbert later named “electric” effects after the Greek word for amber. Amber rubbed that way picks up a negative amount of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of matter, measured in coulombs, that comes in positive and negative kinds.

tossups.p: Bringing a rubbed plastic rod near a metal sphere, without touching it, pulls the opposite kind of this property toward the near side, a process called induction. In a gold-leaf electroscope, two thin strips of gold spread apart when they carry the same kind of this property.
tossups.r: It is measured in coulombs. For 10 points, name this property that protons and electrons carry in equal and opposite amounts.

tossups.p: Robert Millikan won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics partly for measuring the smallest free amount of this property, about 1.6 times ten to the negative nineteenth coulombs. He found it by balancing tiny oil drops in an electric field between two metal plates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that protons carry in a positive form and electrons in a negative form.

tossups.p: This property is quantized, meaning that every free particle or object carries a whole-number multiple of the amount on one proton. An atom becomes an ion when it gains or loses electrons and ends up with a net amount of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, which comes in positive and negative kinds.

tossups.p: Electric current is the rate at which this property flows, so one ampere equals one coulomb of it passing a point each second. Lightning strikes when huge amounts of this property built up in a storm cloud jump to the ground or to another cloud.
tossups.r: Like kinds of it repel. For 10 points, name this property of matter, measured in coulombs.

tossups.p: Any extra amount of this property placed on a metal object spreads out over the object’s outer surface. A Van de Graaff [“van duh GRAHF”] generator piles up so much of this property on its metal dome that it can make a person’s hair stand on end.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, that makes objects with the same kind repel.

tossups.p: The triboelectric [“TRY-boh-ih-LEK-trik”] series ranks materials by whether they tend to gain or lose electrons when rubbed together, which decides what kind of this property each one ends up with. Rubbing a balloon on your hair builds up a static amount of this property on the balloon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in coulombs, that can be positive or negative.

tossups.p: In 1897, J. J. Thomson measured the ratio of this property to mass for the particles in cathode rays, which turned out to be electrons. In 1932, James Chadwick discovered a particle in the nucleus that has none of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which is positive for protons and negative for electrons.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin’s famous 1752 kite experiment is said to have drawn this property from a storm cloud down a wet string to a metal key, where Franklin stored it in a Leyden jar. Franklin also gave the names “positive” and “negative” to the two kinds of this property.
tossups.r: Its SI unit is the coulomb. For 10 points, name this property, whose opposite kinds attract each other.

tossups.p: A capacitor’s capacitance equals the amount of this property stored on one plate divided by the voltage across the plates. An electric field is defined as the force on a small test object divided by the amount of this property it carries.
tossups.r: Protons carry a positive amount of it. For 10 points, name this property, symbolized q and measured in coulombs.

trap.title: Charge, not current
trap.body: Electric charge is the stuff itself, measured in coulombs; electric current is how fast it flows, measured in amperes; and voltage is the push that moves it. Tossups about Millikan’s oil drops can also tempt you to say “electrons” or “elementary charge,” but when the giveaway asks for the property that comes in positive and negative kinds, the answer is just charge.
trap.fix: Coulombs, q, “positive and negative,” “like kinds repel,” conservation, and quantization mean charge. Amperes, ammeters, and I mean current; volts mean voltage. The elementary charge (about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs) is one specific amount of it, not the property itself.
